body.text: Beijing Scan is ORF’s monthly insight on China, analysing crucial political, economic, foreign policy, and military developments.

China has not been immune to the consequences of the Middle East conflict. Disruptions to energy supply chains, coupled with weak domestic economic indicators, continue to weigh on its economy. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has revised China’s growth forecast down from 4.6 percent to 4.5 percent in 2026 and from 4.1 percent to 4.0 percent in 2027. Higher energy costs and continued weakness in China’s domestic economy drove this revision.
As Figure 1 shows, this downward trend, driven by external shocks, is a new development in the post-COVID era.
Figure 1: China’s Real GDP Growth (annual percent change)
Source: Author-generated based on IMF Data Mapper 2026

China’s Producer Price Index (PPI) rose by 5 percent year-on-year in September 2026, its fastest increase in four years, driven by rising commodity and energy prices. Higher raw material costs, supply-chain disruptions, and geopolitical tensions have pushed up factory-gate prices. This could signal mounting consumer inflationary pressures, which weak domestic demand has so far kept in check by limiting companies’ ability to pass on higher costs. China’s continued trade surplus may offer some cushion, but sustained producer-price inflation could eventually push consumer prices higher.
Figure 2: China’s Economy (September 2026)

China’s monthly trade surplus widened to a record US$ 133.53 billion in September 2026, up from US$ 119.1 billion in August. The increase stemmed from a 36.3 percent year-on-year surge in exports to US$ 447.18 billion, largely fuelled by the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom and strong demand for semiconductors and green-technology products. Bloomberg reported that the surplus included US$ 35 billion with the European Union (EU). Predictably, between January and September, China’s cumulative trade surplus reached US$ 938.11 billion, putting it on course to surpass US$ 1 trillion by year-end and potentially match or exceed the US$ 1.189 trillion recorded in 2025.

Between 23 and 25 September, Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met in Washington and secured much-needed policy stability between the world’s two largest economies. The two agreed to extend their trade truce until January 2027, grant favourable tariffs on roughly US$ 30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction, deepen agricultural cooperation, expand Chinese purchases of US energy and a dialogue on AI regulation. The visit operationalised the US–China Board of Trade to discuss tariff reduction and the US–China Board of Investment for further bilateral economic negotiations.

Beijing also stepped up trade and investment engagement with key partners. On 28 September, China and Canada held the first meeting of the Investment Working Group, under their Joint Economic and Trade Commission, in Ottawa to strengthen bilateral investment cooperation. In addition, China and the EU reached an arrangement on vehicle trade, including a reported quota of 350,000 Chinese hybrid-vehicle exports for 2027, to ease trade tensions and give exporters greater certainty. Meanwhile, after Prime Minister Narendra Modi met President Xi at the BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India and China expressed commitment to addressing trade imbalances, supply-chain concerns and market-access issues through bilateral dialogue.

Both US–China summits in May and September 2026 emerged as major events, especially for Taiwan. Taiwanese scholars viewed the meetings as efforts to stabilise bilateral relations rather than end strategic competition. Both governments faced domestic political pressures: the US was approaching its midterm elections, while China was preparing for the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party. Their priority was to reduce external uncertainties while preserving economic and diplomatic engagement. In Taiwan, the summits were seen as “strategic stability at the top, pragmatic engagement at the working level” (上層務虛，底下求實), an unstable truce, and not a lasting reconciliation.
Image 1: Xi meets Trump
Source: Kyodo News

Although initial concerns in Taipei centred on whether Taiwan might become a bargaining chip, economic and trade negotiations proved more substantive. Washington did not proactively raise Taiwan at either summit or adopt Beijing’s framing in May, suggesting that China failed to secure the policy adjustment it sought. Nevertheless, Beijing can gain strategically by portraying American support for Taiwan as weakening, thereby legitimising its preferred interpretation of Cross-Strait relations and the post-war regional order.
Image 2: Xi and Trump in White House
Source: GV Wire

Taipei distinguishes such narrative-building from substantive changes in US policy. Despite Trump’s silence on Taiwan during the summits, continuing arms sales and security cooperation remain stronger indicators of Washington’s commitments. Reported US arms sales totalled approximately US$ 18.6 billion during Trump’s first term, while planned sales under his second term reportedly reached US$ 31.1 billion. Taiwan therefore believes Washington’s strategic focus on the First Island Chain and continuing cooperation with Taipei matter more than summit rhetoric alone.

In autumn 2027, the 21st National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP Party Congress), a once-every-five-years event, will be held in China. Preparations for the Party Congress officially began in March 2026 after the “Two Sessions” concluded, and the meeting is expected to oversee the largest reshuffling of China’s leadership in its history. Over two-thirds of China’s Central Committee and Politburo members will be replaced, mostly due to age limits and longstanding institutional requirements, especially since Xi has reinforced strict party self-discipline (从严治党).

At the 2022 Party Congress, the age threshold for retirement from senior leadership positions was effectively set at those born before 1955. For the upcoming Congress, this threshold is expected to shift to 1960, with those born before that year likely to retire. As the Congress approaches, China has seen significant turnover in both the military and civilian leadership. The military has already lost much of its senior leadership, with most positions under temporary charge. Meanwhile, the civilian leadership has undergone major purges, reshuffles and new appointments. In September, the Party appointed six new provincial Party secretaries, the highest-ranking CCP officials in China’s provinces, as shown in Images 1 and 2. All six were born after 1960 and are therefore likely to remain in office beyond the next Party Congress.
Image 3: Party Secretaries of Tibet, Gansu and Qinghai
Source: Caixin
Image 4: Party Secretaries of Anhui, Henan and Fujian

Alongside the appointments, purges and expulsions have continued. In September, Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli were expelled from the CCP and the military following formal investigations. The official findings cited serious disciplinary violations, including disloyalty, forming political cliques, accepting substantial bribes, and using their positions to secure promotions for others. Several civilian officials also faced disciplinary action, including Sun Shaocheng, the former party secretary of Inner Mongolia, who was expelled from the CCP and dismissed from public office. As the 21st Party Congress approaches, this turnover in the party’s senior ranks is likely to continue, although its pace and scale will depend on the leadership’s personnel decisions and ongoing disciplinary investigations.

On 15 September, a Chinese law titled “Regulations of the State Council on Exit and Entry Administration”, also known as Decree No. 841, took effect. This law allows Beijing to stop Chinese citizens and foreign nationals from leaving the country for a range of vaguely defined reasons related to national security and perceived risks. The law has 19 articles, with Articles 4 and 5 appearing particularly important.
Image 5: Founders of Manus when detained in China
Source: Money Control

Article 4 states: “If a Chinese citizen violates export control or technology import and export regulations that may endanger national industrial or technological security”, they will be prohibited from leaving the country. An early indication of how the law could be used came in April 2026, when China barred Xiao Hong and Ji Yichao, co-founders of Manus, a Singapore-based AI company, from leaving the country after they decided to sell the company to the US technology giant Meta (formerly Facebook). The restrictions were lifted only after the deal was rescinded. The law now formalises such state intervention, giving Beijing a legal basis to prevent the transfer abroad of emerging technologies and key personnel it considers vital to China’s economic future.
Figure 3: China’s Exit Control Law
Source: Author-generated based on the Chinese decree no. 841

Similarly, Article 5 allows Chinese authorities to prevent foreign nationals from leaving the country on a range of vaguely defined grounds. These restrictions could further narrow the space for free expression and academic exchange, encouraging both Chinese citizens and foreigners to practise self-censorship for fear of being barred from leaving China.

On 29 September, the China–Laos Joint Support and Training Centre at Ban Keun Airport in Laos’s Vientiane Province became operational. Beijing has also established an aviation academy at the site, located approximately 50 kilometres north of Vientiane. Both states will jointly maintain and operate these institutions and the base. Satellite imagery indicates that a large, paved runway, a parallel taxiway, and aircraft aprons were under construction at this location.
Image 6: Ban Keun Airbase Developed by China
Source: Vantor

Although Beijing maintains that the aviation infrastructure will train Lao Air Force personnel, the facility’s potential logistical functions appear similar to those of China’s overseas base in Djibouti. Unlike the joint support and training facility at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base, the Laos complex appears to be a larger overseas military presence, which could mark a substantial expansion of China’s military footprint in Southeast Asia and heighten security concerns for Thailand, Vietnam and other regional actors.
Image 7: Air Distance from Ban Keun Chinese Base
Source: Author created through Google Earth

The Chinese base near Vientiane offers Beijing a new military foothold closer to the Indian Ocean approaches than its other established bases. Unlike China’s naval facility at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base and its outposts in the Spratly Islands, Ban Keun could expand China’s access to mainland Southeast Asia and support air-force training and logistics. For India, its significance lies in the potential to strengthen China’s operational reach towards the eastern Indian Ocean and the Strait of Malacca.

From 17 to 21 September, China’s 48th Naval Escort Task Force, comprising the PLA Navy destroyer Tangshan, frigate Daqing, and supply ship Taihu, visited Chittagong, Bangladesh, on its return voyage from the Gulf of Aden. The five-day visit included professional exchanges, ship visits, engagements with Bangladeshi naval personnel, visits to naval facilities and the Bangladesh Naval Academy, and a passage exercise (PASSEX) on departure. These activities reinforced bilateral naval contacts and gave both navies opportunities to build operational familiarity in the Bay of Bengal.
Image 8: China’s 48th Task Force in Chittagong
Source: DefenseDTB

The visit follows a recurring pattern of Chinese naval engagement, evident in similar port calls in 2017, 2020 and 2024, which reflects a deepening professional and military relationship. The anticipated acquisition of Chinese J-10CE fighters would further deepen this relationship. Repeated port calls allow the PLAN to familiarise itself with regional ports and operating conditions, potentially facilitating future logistical cooperation.

Further, China’s role in constructing Bangladesh’s BNS Pekua submarine base and supplying submarines and other military equipment adds another layer. Dhaka’s requirements for training, spare parts, maintenance, and technical support, coupled with these recurring naval visits, defence procurement and Chinese involvement in military infrastructure, point to a denser network of strategic and defence ties around Chittagong and the Bay of Bengal.

Authored by Atul Kumar, Fellow – National Security and China Studies at the Strategic Studies Programme; Jhanvi Tripathi, Associate Fellow – Geoeconomics Programme and Coordinator for the Think20 India Secretariat; and Chieh-Ju Chen (Nikita), Research Intern, Observer Research Foundation (ORF). The views expressed are those of the authors.
